name: TLV9061IDBVR
title: TLV9061, TLV9062, TLV9064 10 MHz rail-to-rail CMOS op amps, with shutdown versions
summary: Single, dual and quad CMOS operational amplifiers for 1.8 V to 5.5 V supplies, with inputs that reach 100 mV past both rails and outputs that swing to the rails. They give 10 MHz gain bandwidth and 6.5 V/µs slew rate on 538 µA per channel, with 0.5 pA input bias current and 10 nV/√Hz broadband noise. They are unity-gain stable, drive 100 pF directly, include an RFI and EMI filter and do not phase-reverse. The S versions add active-low shutdown that drops the supply current below 1 µA and leaves the output high impedance.

circuits.title: Single-pole low-pass filter with gain
circuits.description: R1 and C1 form a first-order RC low-pass ahead of the noninverting input; the amplifier then gains the filtered signal by 1 + RF / RG, with RG from the inverting input to ground and RF from the output back to it. The corner sits at 1 / (2π R1 C1).

circuits.title: Low-side current sense
circuits.description: The load current returns to ground through a 0.1 Ω shunt; the drop across it, up to 100 mV at 1 A, goes to the noninverting input. RF = 165 kΩ and RG = 3.4 kΩ set a noninverting gain of about 49.5 V/V, so the output spans roughly 0 V to 4.95 V for 0 A to 1 A. The amplifier runs from 5 V with V– at ground.
notes: Design targets: load current 0 A to 1 A, output 4.95 V full scale, shunt voltage at most 100 mV.

circuits.title: Inverting comparator
circuits.description: One channel of a TLV9062 runs open loop as a comparator. Two 100 kΩ resistors split the 5 V supply into a 2.5 V threshold on the noninverting input, and the input signal (0 V to 5 V) drives the inverting input. Below the threshold the output goes to the positive rail; above it the output goes to the negative rail.
notes: Only channel 1 of the TLV9062 is used in this circuit.

circuits.title: Series input resistor for overload current limiting
circuits.description: A unity-gain follower whose noninverting input is fed through a 5 kΩ resistor. When the input is driven past a supply rail, the resistor holds the current through the internal clamp diodes to the 10 mA limit. The resistor adds thermal noise at the input.

circuits.title: Two noninverting amplifiers (layout example)
circuits.description: Both channels of a TLV9062 are noninverting amplifiers: each input signal goes straight to IN+, RG runs from IN– to ground and RF from IN– to the output. A ceramic bypass capacitor sits at each supply pin, from V+ to ground and from V– to ground, as near the package as possible.
notes: C1 and C2 are 0.1 µF low-ESR ceramic capacitors, one at each supply pin.
A ground plane lies on another layer.

operation.text: TLV9061 is the single, TLV9062 the dual and TLV9064 the quad version; TLV9061S, TLV9062S and TLV9064S add shutdown pins. All are unity-gain stable CMOS amplifiers with rail-to-rail inputs and outputs, an internal RFI/EMI filter, and no output phase reversal when the inputs are overdriven.
The amplifiers work from 1.8 V to 5.5 V total (±0.9 V to ±2.75 V split). More than 6 V across the supply pins can destroy the part. Many limits hold over –40°C to 125°C.
The amplifier drives 100 pF directly. Its open-loop output impedance is resistive, which makes larger capacitive loads easier to stabilize.

The common-mode range runs 100 mV past both rails at any supply from 1.8 V to 5.5 V. Two input pairs share the job: a P-channel pair from 200 mV below V– up to about (V+) – 1.4 V, and an N-channel pair from about (V+) – 1.4 V to 200 mV above V+. Both pairs conduct in a band typically (V+) – 1.2 V to (V+) – 1 V; with process spread the band can sit anywhere from (V+) – 1.4 V to (V+) – 1.2 V at the low end up to (V+) – 1 V to (V+) – 0.8 V at the high end. Offset, drift, PSRR, CMRR and THD are worse inside that band.
A class AB output with common-source transistors swings to within 15 mV of either rail into 10 kΩ, whatever the supply. Other loads change how close it gets to the rails.

When the output saturates against a rail, the output transistors need time to leave saturation before the amplifier slews again; that recovery is about 200 ns. The total delay out of an overload is the recovery time plus the slewing time.

On the S versions an active-low SHDN pin puts the amplifier into standby, drawing typically under 1 µA. The pin is a high-impedance CMOS input referred to V–; its threshold is about 800 mV above V– whatever the supply, with hysteresis. Logic low is V– to V– + 0.2 V and logic high is V– + 1.2 V to V+; the pin must be driven or tied, never left open. Each channel of the dual has its own pin; the quad's channels switch in pairs (1-2 and 3-4). Enabling from full shutdown takes 10 µs and disabling 3 µs. A disabled output is high impedance, so outputs can share a bus. Turn-off time grows with load resistance: the specified time assumes 10 kΩ to VS / 2, and with no load it is much longer.
The parts run whenever the supply is between 1.8 V and 5.5 V. The S versions shut down while a valid logic low sits on the shutdown pin.

Put 0.1 µF bypass capacitors close to the supply pins to keep noise from noisy or high-impedance supplies out of the circuit. Use low-ESR ceramic parts, one from each supply pin to ground; a single capacitor from V+ to ground covers a single-supply design.

Every pin has ESD protection; on the inputs and output it is mostly steering diodes to the supply pins. These diodes also protect against input overdrive as long as the current stays at 10 mA or below. A series resistor in the driven input limits that current, at the cost of extra thermal noise, so keep it small where noise matters.

The TLV9062 can compare two voltages applied to its inputs with no feedback. It does not phase-reverse over the full common-mode range, which extends 100 mV past the rails. Propagation delay is the overload recovery time plus the slewing time; overdrive below 100 mV lengthens it, because recovery slows and slew rate drops.

Gain depends only on the ratio RF / RG. The absolute values set the impedance level, which decides supply current drain and how much stray capacitance matters; there is no single best level, so pick it for the system.

Keep analog and digital grounds separate and watch where ground current flows; a ground plane on one or more layers spreads heat and cuts EMI pickup. Route inputs away from supply and output traces, crossing noisy traces at 90° if they must cross. Place RF and RG and other parts tight to the package so the inverting node carries little parasitic capacitance, and keep input traces short. Guarding sensitive traces with a ring held at low impedance cuts leakage from nearby traces at other voltages.
Clean the board after assembly. Moisture taken into the plastic package can shift precision parts, so after any aqueous wash bake the assembly; 30 minutes at 85°C is usually enough.

The DSG and RTE packages have an exposed pad underneath that must be soldered to the board for heat and mechanical strength; thermal vias can tie it to a copper plane. The RTE pad is 1.66 ± 0.10 mm square.
